rv.q: The result is funny and insightful in its attempt to reconcile the notion of marriage and sexual attraction.
Cattrall and Gross make emotional bipolarity seem charming as they flop around the pasha beds in Amanda's flat.

Cattrall reaffirms her considerable talent. Her Amanda has emotional nuance, vulnerability and odd, unexpectedly humanizing glimmers of a common touch beneath the cultivated veneer of exquisite boredom and petulance...Canadian actor Gross is every bit Cattrall's equal.
Mr. Eyre's production convincingly stakes a claim not only for Ms. Cattrall as a skillfully pliable actress but also for the bubbly pleasures forever on tap in 'Private Lives.'
For most of his life, Noël Coward was widely regarded as a theatrical lightweight, albeit a brilliant one.
Those critical of star-casting on Broadway should catch Kim Cattrall — the single best thing in the humdrum new revival of Noël Coward's "Private Lives" that opened last night.
Watching actors who don’t meld on that deep, cellular level is equally unbearable.
The production succeeds in large part because of the casting of Kim Cattrall and Paul Gross.
For the most part, Coward's louche shenanigans feel remarkably modern.
Amanda and Elyot enjoy each other as much as they annoy each other, and the performers' playful rapport makes their guilty pleasure infectious.
Yet Richard Eyre's production largely fails to land even the easy laughs.
Cattrall, in her mid-50s, looks great and handles an English accent effortlessly, but she has trouble locating Amanda's dryness and mercurial whimsy.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this polished but uneven revival, with Kim Cattrall earning praise for her sophisticated performance while some find Richard Eyre's naturalistic direction drains the comedy of its sparkle.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
